definition: Solution dyeing colors a manufactured fiber by adding pigment or dye to the polymer melt or spinning solution (the dope) before extrusion, so color is distributed through the fiber.
explanation: In conventional dyeing, color diffuses into a finished fiber, yarn or fabric from a water bath. In solution dyeing, colorant, usually an insoluble pigment dispersed with a carrier or dispersant, is metered into the molten polymer in melt spinning or into the dissolved polymer in wet or solvent spinning. The colorant is locked into the polymer matrix as the filament forms. It is established for synthetic polymers such as polyester, nylon and polypropylene, solution-dyed rayon is also produced, and the method is increasingly studied for lyocell-type fibers.
example: A carpet maker compares a solution-dyed nylon and a piece-dyed nylon. After bleach spotting and weeks of sunlight, the solution-dyed sample changes little, while the piece-dyed sample shows a pale mark. Cutting a fiber cross-section reveals why: pigment particles are dispersed throughout the solution-dyed fiber, whereas the piece-dyed fiber's color sits in dye molecules that bleach can attack.
caution: Solution dyeing reduces dyehouse water and effluent but does not make a product environmentally benign overall; pigment production and polymer origin still matter. Color must be chosen at the fiber stage, so small, quick-turnaround batches are harder. Pigments can alter fiber strength and spinning behavior. The term applies to manufactured fibers, not to cotton, wool or silk.
deeper: Success depends on pigment particle size and dispersion stability in the dope. Agglomerates block spinneret holes and create weak points, so dispersants are designed to keep particles well below filament dimensions; one viscose study reports carbon black dispersed near 160 nm and fibers with colorfastness above grade 4. In lyocell, about 0.5 percent carbon black raised breaking strength, while 2 percent reduced it slightly. Dope dyeing polylactic acid avoids the hydrolytic degradation that high-temperature exhaust dyeing causes. Forensic microscopy of 76 solution-dyed fibers found one to six pigments per fiber, with distinct particle morphologies and about 40 percent fluorescing. Recycling studies show dope-dyed cellulosic fibers can be regenerated with a color shift of Delta E below 1 using NMMO-lyocell or Ioncell routes.
origins: The word dope is the trade name for a spinning solution, so dope-dyed describes coloring at that stage. Adding colorant before extrusion became established for synthetic polymers, where melt or solution spinning offers a natural mixing point, while researchers note that spin dyeing remains uncommon for man-made cellulosic fibers. Recent work extends it to lyocell-type and bio-based fibers and examines its role in fiber recycling.

definition: Solution spinning makes fibers from polymers that cannot be melted without degrading, by dissolving them into a viscous dope, extruding it and removing the solvent by evaporation or coagulation.
explanation: There are three main variants. In wet spinning the spinneret sits in a coagulation bath of nonsolvent, where the polymer precipitates as filaments; acrylic, modacrylic, viscose rayon and some aramids are made this way. In dry spinning the dope is extruded into a heated, gas-filled chamber and the solvent evaporates; cellulose acetate is traditionally dry spun from acetone, and spandex is generally dry spun. In dry-jet wet (air-gap) spinning the jets cross a short air gap before entering the bath, so they can be stretched while still fluid; para-aramid and lyocell are made this way.
example: A student compares fiber cross-sections under a microscope. Regular viscose shows a serrated outline, formed as its skin set first in the bath; dry-spun acetate shows a lobed outline; air-gap-spun lyocell is close to round. Each shape records how quickly, and from which direction, solvent left the forming filament.
caution: Solution spinning names a family of processes, not a fiber. The solvent, its hazards and its recovery rate shape much of the environmental profile, and they vary widely: amine oxide for lyocell, acetone for acetate, amide solvents such as dimethylacetamide for spandex, concentrated sulfuric acid for para-aramid. Do not confuse it with solution dyeing, which adds pigment to the dope.
deeper: In wet spinning, solvent diffuses out while nonsolvent diffuses in, so a skin forms before the core solidifies; this diffusion balance controls voids and cross-section. Dry spinning is limited by evaporation rate and requires solvent recovery. Dry-jet wet spinning separates spinneret and bath by an air gap, typically about 0.1 to 10 cm in aramid patents, and stretching in the gap orients the molecules. Para-aramid dope in concentrated sulfuric acid is liquid crystalline: rodlike chains align into a nematic phase, and viscosity can fall as concentration rises. Lyocell dissolves cellulose in N-methylmorpholine N-oxide and water, and solvent recovery above 99 percent is reported for the process.
origins: Solution spinning predates melt spinning: the first artificial silks of the late nineteenth century were extruded from cellulose solutions. A key later advance came at DuPont, where Stephanie Kwolek found in 1965 that a para-aramid formed an unusual cloudy, liquid-crystalline solution, and Herbert Blades developed the dry-jet wet process that spun such dopes into high-modulus fiber. Lyocell later applied the air-gap method to cellulose dissolved directly in an organic solvent.
